papers.title: Extending indoor airborne infection risk modelling to 3D, with local surface deposition
papers.abstract: Mathematical models of indoor disease transmission often rely on simplifying assumptions to reduce computational cost. In particular, in the Viral Infection Risk Indoor Simulator (VIRIS)[13], which combines architectural layout, people movement and airborne viral transmission, aerosol concentrations are assumed uniform across room height, allowing a two-dimensional (2D) formulation. Also, particle deposition on surfaces is represented by a first-order removal term acting throughout the computational domain. Here, we extend VIRIS to the VIRIS-3D-L framework to investigate how these two assumptions affect the predicted infection risk. In VIRIS-3D-L, we solve the reaction-diffusion equation in three dimensions (3D), and aerosol deposition is represented by local surface removal through a Robin boundary condition. We compare VIRIS with VIRIS-3D-L across three indoor settings of increasing architectural and people-movement complexity: a courtroom, a care home, and a supermarket. For the courtroom, care home, and supermarket, respectively, at the end of the simulation, the original 2D formulation with global removal predicts average infection risks across individuals of 44%, 78%, and 25%, while VIRIS-3D-L predicts risks of 51%, 85%, and 28%. Thus, VIRIS significantly underestimates infection risk in all three settings. The predictions of VIRIS-3D-L also show agreement with a documented courtroom outbreak that was used to validate VIRIS. Although computation time increases by approximately a factor of four on average, simulations remain feasible on a standard laptop, taking between eight minutes and just under 1.5 hours. These findings suggest that VIRIS-3D-L offers a more physically realistic framework for assessing indoor airborne infection risk in indoor spaces without prohibitive computational costs.
